title: Longest Evenly Mixed Slice
statement:
You get a string s made only of the letters 'a', 'b' and 'c'. Call a contiguous slice of s evenly mixed when every letter that appears in it appears the same number of times. Letters that do not appear at all are ignored, so "bb", "acca" and "cab" are all evenly mixed, while "aab" is not.

Return the length of the longest evenly mixed slice.

examples.why: "abba" has two a's and two b's. Adding the c would need a second c to stay even.
The run "bbbb" uses one letter, which counts as evenly mixed. No slice with an a does better.
The whole string has three of each letter, even though no shorter prefix is balanced.

hints: Split the problem by which letters appear in the slice: one letter, exactly two letters, or all three.

For two letters x and y, a slice is even when count(x) − count(y) is the same at both ends of the slice. The same trick as "longest slice with equal 0s and 1s". But the third letter must not appear inside the slice.
For all three letters, use the pair (count(a) − count(b), count(b) − count(c)) as the key. Store the first index where each key appears; a repeat of a key at index i closes an even slice.

explain.intuition:
Comparing counts inside every slice is O(n²). The usual way out is prefix counts: a slice (j, i] has equal counts of x and y exactly when count(x) − count(y) has the same value after j and after i. So the longest such slice ends at i and starts right after the first index where that difference was seen.

The catch is that "every letter that appears" changes with the slice. So handle the three shapes separately and take the best. One letter: the longest run. Two letters x and y: the difference trick, but restarted every time the third letter shows up, because the slice must not contain it. All three letters: two differences at once, (a − b, b − c), as one hash key. A repeated key means all three counts grew by the same amount, and since the slice is non-empty that amount is at least 1, so every letter really appears.
steps: One letter: scan once and record the longest run of equal characters.

For each pair (x, y) with third letter z: keep diff and a map first starting as {0: −1}. At index i, if s[i] = z reset diff = 0 and first = {0: i}. Otherwise update diff; if it is in first, the slice i − first[diff] is a candidate, else store first[diff] = i.
For all three letters: keep first for the key (a − b, b − c), starting with the key (0, 0) at index −1, and do the same lookup at every index without any resets.
pitfalls: Skipping the third letter instead of resetting at it. In "acccb" the a–b difference returns to 0 at the end, which claims the whole string, yet it holds three c's and one a. The answer is 3 ("ccc").
Storing the latest index of each key instead of the first, which finds the shortest even slice rather than the longest.
Forgetting the single-letter case: "cbaaaaaaa" is won by a run of a's.

solutions.title: Count every slice
solutions.idea: Fix the start, extend the end, keep three counters and check that the non-zero ones are equal.

solutions.title: Three shapes, prefix differences
solutions.idea: Runs for one letter; a difference map reset at the third letter for each pair; a two-difference key for all three letters.

followups: The string may now use all 26 letters, with n ≤ 1000. Which approach still works, and how fast is it?
Return how many evenly mixed slices there are instead of the longest one.
